newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britannia steams into Hong Kong for farewell.
newsitem.headline: Britannia steams into Hong Kong for farewell.

text.p: The royal yacht Britannia steamed into Hong Kong on Monday, adding more than a touch of class to a harbour teeming with freighters, ferries, junks and sampans.

Like an ageing but still elegant actress, the 44-year-old yacht has been summoned to play a character role in the historic drama of Hong Kong's June 30 return to China after more than 150 years under British rule.

The 412-foot, three-masted ship is to serve as temporary home for Prince Charles, the heir to the British throne, during the handover festivities. The prince, who will formally hand back the territory to Chinese President Jiang Zemin, is due in Hong Kong at the weekend.
Britannia tied up close to the spot where the Union Jack will be lowered for the last time in Hong Kong at sunset next Monday.
Before then the yacht will host a number of dinners, parties and high-level meetings.
Finally the prince and Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten will sail away together on Britannia in the pre-dawn dark on July 1.
Sailors and Royal Marines were busy on Monday painting the hull and polishing the brass to get the ship in shape for her guests.
Seaman "Peddler" Palmer was using a bottle of Goddard's Long-term Brass and Copper Polish and lots of elbow grease to buff up deck and rail fittings, as he does most days for two or three hours.
"Sure it gets boring at times, especially when it rains right after you've done your work," Palmer said. "Most of the time the duty's fun."
A tour of the ship including the royal apartments revealed that Britannia is everything Hong Kong is not.
More state of the ark than state of the art, the yacht is understated and comfortable but not glitzy. There's the faint whiff of very old money rather than the reek of new.
Britannia's faded, end-of-empire look, reminiscent of 1950s Bermuda, contrasts sharply with the glittering office towers and hotels which loom above it in Hong Kong's central district.

The Queen's office is a modest room with blond mahogany furnishings and an antique telephone system referred to as "the dictaphone" whose only virtue is that it's like the one in Buckingham Palace in London.
The ship's steam engine was pulled from a British submarine in 1943. It's a museum piece, the polished copper tubing making it look more like part of a brewery than the business end of a ship.

Among those greeting the royal yacht on Monday were "Side-party Jenny", an ancient Chinese woman who has been a part of work parties scrubbing the sides of British vessels in Hong Kong since the 1930s.

Crew members familiar with Jenny from previous voyages to Hong Kong greeted her at the pier. Asked if she would be scrubbing Britannia, Jenny replied in perfect British English: "Might be, but I don't know yet since we didn't see the Captain yet."
Britannia was launched in 1953 and has steamed well over a million miles during her career. The ship is scheduled to be decommissioned at the end of 1997 and there are no plans to replace her.
